content: I can appreciate (and even enjoy) some AI songs, but I just can't get the same emotional connection to them as I do from art created by humans. My favorite music producers all have creative ways of making their music sound more "human". You might not even realize it's there, but you can feel the difference without it. For example: 1. Many hip-hop artists find beats made in software like Ableton or FL Studio to be too "stiff". When all of the snares or kicks are perfectly on beat, it feels robotic. Producers will intentionally make things slightly off-beat (e.g. physically playing drum pads where there is some room for human error) so the beat has more "swing". 2. We've had digital music for decades, and yet producers will still add in the crackling sound effect of a record player needle hitting the vinyl. If you really listen, you'll hear this in the back of tons of R&B and acoustic songs. 3. Even for electronic music, producers will take the raw computer generated noises and add tons of artificial distortion to make them have more "texture". Some will even take a voice note on their phone of a loud thud noise, and then tweak the EQ and filters to make that be the kick drum, instead of using a fully digital sound. 4. When you are recording real instruments, like putting a microphone up to a guitar, you can also capture other sounds in the room. You'll notice on older records there are often mistakes or strange sounds captured in the recording that they end up keeping in. Ironically these have ended up being some of the most iconic parts of songs. For example, in the song "(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay", the iconic whistling that Otis Redding does at the end was supposed to be a placeholder for an outro, but he unfortunately died in a plane crash days after recording it. The whistling was my favorite part before I even knew that anecdote. This same thing applies to most art, like images or movies. Think about why Christopher Nolan records all of his movies on film with these massive, expensive, difficult to use IMAX cameras. He truly believes the audience can feel the difference and goes to great lengths to preserve that artistry. So, can a robot write a symphony? Yes. Is it the same as what human artists can do? No. We may train AI on all of these patterns. AI might come up with new types of art we haven't thought of before! But humans will continue to have an ingenuity and creativity that is unique. I will enjoy the slopcore AI songs about eating KFC chicken and also continue to be an avid concert goer and movie enjoyer. Media

More hardcore engineering teams are realizing how important it is to own the harness. I expect more full-stack AI companies to follow. Ramp quickly realized they could move faster and better with their agent harness. When you own the harness, you can co-evolve it to meet your needs. The foundations don't change much; only the tooling and behavior need extending, so make the harness malleable from the start. Great application of small language models by Meta. They find that an 8B model picks tools better than a 402B model when trained for the job. This work focuses on tool selection for agents with more than ten thousand tools. At that scale, tool descriptions won't fit in context, and a retriever can only rank candidates without knowing which tools the instruction actually needs. Many systems hand this step to a proprietary LLM. They train Qwen3 models on a Plan, Retrieve, Select workflow. The model splits the instruction into substeps, the retriever returns candidates for each one, and the model commits one tool per substep. Training is SFT on about 20K curated ToolBench instructions, then RL with a reward that scores how many gold tools are covered and at what rank. On ToolBench G3, the 8B model goes from 36.2% after SFT to 41.5% after RL, above prompted Llama-4-Maverick. The trained selector also works with different retrievers and on tool corpora from new domains. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31483 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/training-small-language-models-for-transferable-tool-selection-2610.31483

RAG is so back! This work shows that plain RAG over raw chat history beats complex agentic memory systems on most long-term memory benchmarks. (bookmark it) They tested Raw-RAG, which is just dense retrieval plus reranking over the raw conversation, feeding a reader LLM. Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MEME and MemoryAgentBench, it ranks first in six of seven benchmark and model settings, ahead of the strongest agentic memory system by 0.13 to 5.53 points. Ingestion on BEAM-1M takes 0.3 hours, against 3.2 to 27 hours for systems like Mem0, MemOS and Memora. Why does it hold up? Raw history keeps more of the evidence a question needs, including the relations and dependency paths behind an answer. Rewriting history into memory entries tends to drop those important bits. Even with complete access to the transformed memory stores, models answer less accurately than with raw evidence. Before adding a memory layer to your agent, at least run this baseline on your own data. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30755 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/is-complex-agentic-memory-always-needed-naive-rag-is-stronger-than-we-thought-2610.30755

The question I get more than any other on strategy calls is: how often should we be emailing? Every answer I’ve ever given has been a compromise. Three a week is too much for some people on your list and nowhere near enough for the ones who’d happily hear from you twice that often. So you pick a number in the middle and accept that it’s wrong for most of them. We call that a sending strategy. @getallanai handles it per person instead. You set a floor and a ceiling. Minimum one a week, maximum four, whatever you’re comfortable with. Then it decides where each subscriber sits inside that range, and what time of day to reach them. Someone opening everything and browsing twice a week gets four. Someone drifting off gets one. Same list, same flow, the frequency just stops being one number you applied to everybody. It runs on top of Omnisend or Klaviyo, so none of this means moving your program. Point it at one trigger and leave it for a month. It’s free for 30 days, and the trial includes the creative, so there’s nothing to build and nothing to pay before you find out what your single number has been costing you. Really digging this new arc of specialized RL models. Bullish on this effort to understand and unlock collective intelligence. Highly recommend checking out the technical report. RLCR is just one of the latest efforts to train LLMs as agent organizations. Why is this a big deal, and why is it necessary? Coordination and organization are important primitives as we move into agentic long-horizon work. Agents should natively support these capabilities, which is mostly done through harnesses today. So far, multi-agent systems and how they coordinate are not well understood. This Avalon-M1-Mini model attempts to study this more closely. I think this could help us understand and discover efficient, safe ways to build effective multi-agent systems for domain-specific problems. Check out how they improve results with an eight-hire organization. Promising results. The safety risks are also worth a closer look. This is small-scale, but as they scale, I am particularly curious about whether optimal and novel organizational designs (hierarchical and coordination strategies) will emerge. I'll take a closer look at this approach and how it applies to automated research. I think there is so much to unlock there. Congrats to my former colleague, @rosstaylor90, and his team. Truly cracked 👏 Introducing Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards (RLCR). RLCR is a recipe that trains language models as agent organisations, which share a message board and workspace.
